The Angel's News to Maryam

The Qur'an speaks of Maryam with the sweetest words: "And when the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you, purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds" (Qur'an 3:42). Maryam had a pure heart, always busy in worshiping her Lord.

Then came the astonishing news. The angels said: "O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you glad tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah — Isa son of Maryam — honored in this world and the Hereafter, and among those near to Allah" (Qur'an 3:45). A baby was coming — with no father.

Maryam was amazed. How could she have a son, when no man had touched her? The answer came: "He said: Thus will it be — your Lord says: It is easy for Me" (Qur'an 3:47). The same Allah who created Adam without a father could create a child for Maryam.

And the angels told what the baby would do: "He will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he will be among the righteous" (Qur'an 3:46). A baby that speaks in the cradle — a sign of Allah to the whole world.

And Allah promised to teach him greatly: "And He will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Injil" (Qur'an 3:48). So Isa would be a special boy with a special book, carrying the light of Allah.
The Birth Under the Palm
Months passed, and the time of the baby came. Maryam walked alone to a quiet, far-away place. The Qur'an says: "So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a place far away" (Qur'an 19:22).
The pain was hard, and Maryam was alone. She cried from her heart: "Ah, would that I had died before this and been a thing forgotten" (Qur'an 19:23).
But the Merciful Lord was with her. A voice came from under the palm: "Do not grieve; your Lord has made a stream beneath you" (Qur'an 19:24). Allah had placed water at the feet of the tired mother.

Then came the wonderful help: "And shake the trunk of the palm tree toward you — it will drop upon you fresh, ripe dates. So eat, drink, and be glad" (Qur'an 19:25–26). The first food of the new mother was sweet dates from the blessed tree.

And when she carried the baby back to her people, they were shocked: "O Maryam, you have brought something unprecedented" (Qur'an 19:27). Then the miracle happened — the baby in the cradle spoke: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" (Qur'an 19:30). The little one spoke the truth.
The Messenger and His Miracles

Isa grew up and became the prophet who was promised to Maryam. Allah gave him a beautiful book, the Injil: "And He will teach him the Book and the wisdom and the Torah and the Injil" (Qur'an 3:48). With the Injil, Isa guided his people back to the truth.

Isa's message was one and clear — worship Allah alone: "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him — this is the straight path" (Qur'an 3:51). He never asked anyone to worship him; he only pointed to his Lord.

Allah gave His messenger beautiful miracles. The Qur'an recalls: "And you heal the blind and the leper by My permission, and you bring the dead to life by My permission" (Qur'an 5:110). The blind saw again, the sick became clean, and the dead returned — all by the power of Allah.

Every miracle had one lesson: the One who does everything is Allah. Isa told his people: Allah created me without a father, so believe in His power, not in me. The miracles were a finger pointing to the sky.
Isa called his people to complete surrender — to Islam. The Qur'an tells us: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam" (Qur'an 3:19). One Lord, one way, and one gift: peace with Allah.
The Table from Heaven

Around Isa gathered faithful friends called the disciples — the Hawariyyun. They loved the Prophet and supported him. When Isa asked for helpers, they answered: "We are the helpers of Allah" (Qur'an 3:52).

One day the disciples made a wonderful request: "O Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table from the sky?" (Qur'an 5:112). They wanted a sign that their eyes could see and their hands could touch.

Isa turned to his Lord and prayed: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from the sky that will be a feast for us, a sign from You, and grant us provision, for You are the best of providers" (Qur'an 5:114).

And the Lord answered. The Qur'an says the table came down from the sky with food from the blessing of Allah, and it became a sign for the believers of every time (Qur'an 5:115). A meal that no kitchen cooked, sent by the Lord of the heavens.
That table taught the disciples a beautiful lesson: the same Allah who sends rain to the earth also spreads a table for His believers. Whoever trusts Him is never hungry in the heart.
The Enemies' Plan

But not everyone believed. The leaders of the city did not like the Prophet who healed the sick and woke the dead. They were afraid, and their hearts filled with hatred. The Qur'an says: "And they planned, and Allah planned, and Allah is the best of planners" (Qur'an 3:54).

The leaders whispered among themselves and spread false words about the Prophet. They called him a magician and told the people not to listen. But the sick who were healed and the poor who were fed knew the truth — Isa was a man of Allah.

Their hatred grew until they decided to do a terrible thing — they wanted to kill the Prophet of Allah. The night came when the cruel people gathered, sure that their plan could not fail. But the Qur'an tells us: the plans of people are nothing beside the plan of Allah.

Later, some of them even claimed: "We have killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah" (Qur'an 4:157). They said it proudly — but their words were only words. The truth was different, and the Qur'an says it in the clearest way.
So the last chapter of the enemies' story was written by Allah, not by them. Let us open the next chapter to see what the Qur'an tells us really happened that night.
Allah Raised Him

Now listen to the truth that the Qur'an tells us. Allah says about that night: "And they did not kill him, and they did not crucify him, but it was made to appear to them" (Qur'an 4:157). The brave words of the enemies were empty — the Prophet of Allah was safe.

Allah does not need soldiers to save His messenger. He simply said the word, and the plan of the enemies fell apart like a house of sand. The people could not touch the Prophet whom Allah was guarding.

Then Allah lifted His messenger to Himself: "Rather, Allah raised him to Himself, and Allah is ever Mighty and Wise" (Qur'an 4:158). The Prophet left this world in the most beautiful way — by rising to his Lord, not by the hands of his enemies.

And the Qur'an adds: "And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death" (Qur'an 4:159). Even those who argued about him will one day see the truth — that Isa was a messenger of Allah, honored and safe.

So the story of that night ends with peace, not sorrow. The enemies were wrong, the believers were right, and the Prophet went home to the mercy of his Lord. Nothing about that night should make a Muslim sad — it was a night of Allah's protection.
The Lesson: Isa, Servant of Allah

Do you want to know who Isa really is? The Qur'an answers with a beautiful comparison: "Indeed, the example of Isa with Allah is like the example of Adam. He created him from dust, then He said to him: Be, and he was" (Qur'an 3:59). Like Adam, Isa was created by the word of Allah.

So Isa is not a god, and he never said he was. The Qur'an says: "The Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, was only a messenger of Allah and His word which He gave to Maryam" (Qur'an 4:171). A beloved prophet — but still a servant of Allah.

The baby in the cradle had already said the same thing: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" (Qur'an 19:30). From the cradle to the sky, Isa's words never changed — he was a servant of his Lord.

And Allah gave him the sweetest greeting: "Peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive" (Qur'an 19:33). A life with peace at its beginning, its end, and its return.

So when you hear about Isa, remember this lesson: he is a prophet of Allah, a servant of his Lord, and a brother of all the messengers. We love him, we honor him, and we follow the truth he brought: worship Allah alone. That is the way of Isa, the way of Islam, and the way of peace.
Makkah Before Islam

Long before Muhammad was born, the city of Makkah stood in a dry valley in the middle of Arabia. Around its heart stood the Kaaba, the first house ever built for the worship of Allah. Pilgrims came from many lands to visit it, and the people of Makkah honored it greatly.

But the people had slowly forgotten the message of Ibrahim, the prophet who built the Kaaba. Around the sacred house they placed icons made of stone and wood, and they stood before these icons asking for what only Allah could give. Their faith had become mixed with carved statues.

Then one year an event shook the whole city. A great army came from Yemen with huge elephants, and it had come to destroy the Kaaba. The people of Makkah could not fight, so they climbed the hills and asked Allah to protect His own sacred house.

Allah answered them in a wonderful way: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the army of the elephant?" (Qur'an 105:1). He sent flocks of birds carrying small stones, and the proud army was scattered. The Kaaba stayed safe.

Into this very city, the city of the sacred house, the final messenger was about to be born. Allah had kept the Quraysh safe and made their trade easy for the home of His house (Qur'an 106:1–4). Makkah was waiting for its greatest child.
The Call Begins

The Prophet began to call his family first, with the softest words. His wife Khadijah, his friend Abu Bakr, his young cousin Ali, and his servant Zayd, they all believed at once. Then the Prophet opened his door to everyone who would listen.

Then Allah commanded him: "And warn your nearest relatives" (Qur'an 26:214). So the Prophet stood on the hill of Safa and called out loudly to the people of Makkah. He asked them: "If I told you an army was coming from behind this hill, would you believe me?" They all said yes, because he was the truthful one.

Then the Prophet said: "I am a warner to you before a great punishment. There is no god but Allah." His uncle Abu Lahab shouted angrily, but others listened with wonder. Slowly, like a small light growing in the dark, the call of Allah spread.

The Prophet never forced anyone. He only spoke the truth with patience, and let the truth speak for itself. Those who listened with an honest heart found the light, and the first believers became the first bricks of the most beautiful building in history, the ummah.
Patience in the Days of Hurt

The people of Makkah did not like the new call. They mocked the Prophet, threw dirt on his path, and hurt the weak believers. But the Prophet never answered hurt with hurt. He stayed gentle, like the Qur'an teaches: "Take what is given with gentleness and turn away from the ignorant" (Qur'an 7:199).

The hardest days came when the enemies of Makkah starved the believers. For two long years the Muslims could not buy food or visit their friends, and they ate the leaves of trees to stay alive. Yet their faith never left them, because their hearts were full of Allah.

In those years, the Prophet lost the two people who loved him most, his dear uncle Abu Talib and his beloved wife Khadijah. The year became known as the year of sorrow. But even in the deepest grief, the Prophet did not complain; he only prayed more.

The Prophet once walked all the way to the city of Ta'if to invite its people to Allah, but they refused and threw stones at him until his blessed feet bled. And then the Prophet prayed: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know." He did not curse the ones who hurt him; he asked Allah to guide them. That is the mercy of Muhammad.

The days of hurt taught the believers the deepest secret of faith: patience is a shield, and forgiveness is a sword of mercy. When the world closes every door, Allah opens the doors of the sky for those who trust Him.
The Orphan Boy of Makkah

Long ago, in the city of Makkah, a baby boy was born whose father had passed away before he was born. His name was Muhammad, which means "the praised one." His grandfather Abdul-Muttalib loved him dearly and took care of him.

Soon his grandfather also passed away, and his kind uncle Abu Talib took him into his home. Muhammad grew up as a gentle boy with a quiet heart, loved by everyone who knew him. He worked as a shepherd, caring for the sheep with mercy.

Allah had not forgotten His beloved orphan. Years later, Allah reminded him of those early days with tender words: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And He found you lost and guided you?" (Qur'an 93:6-7).

The orphan of Makkah became the greatest man in history, because Allah was with him. His childhood teaches every child that even when life is hard and parents are lost, Allah never leaves the one who trusts in Him.
The Truthful and the Trustworthy

Muhammad grew up to be an honest merchant. His words were always true, and his hands were always honest. The people of Makkah gave him two beautiful titles: as-Sadiq, "the truthful," and al-Amin, "the trustworthy."

People would leave their money and their precious things with Muhammad when they traveled, because they knew he would return everything safely. He returned every single thing, and nobody was ever deceived by him.

One day, the tribes of Makkah disagreed about who would place the sacred Black Stone in the Kaaba, and they almost fought. Then someone said: "Let the first man to enter the gate decide." That man was Muhammad, and with his wise hands he placed the stone on a cloth and asked every tribe to carry it together, so that everyone was happy.

Long before the Qur'an came, the people already trusted Muhammad with everything they had. When Allah chose him as a prophet, the first words from the people's hearts were: "We never knew you to lie." Honesty had prepared the way for the truth.
The First Words from Allah

As Muhammad grew older, he loved to be alone and think about the One who made the skies and the earth. He would walk to a quiet cave on Mount Hira, far above the city, and sit there thinking and remembering Allah.

In the year he turned forty, in the month of Ramadan, something wonderful happened in that cave. The angel Jibreel came to him with the first words of the Qur'an: "Read in the name of your Lord who created" (Qur'an 96:1).

Muhammad was amazed and afraid. He hurried home to his dear wife Khadijah, trembling: "Cover me, cover me!" She wrapped him warmly and said the most beautiful words: "Allah will never disgrace you — you keep family ties, you speak the truth, you help the needy."

Khadijah believed him at once. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqah, a wise man who knew the books of Allah. Waraqah heard the story and said: "This is the same angel who came to Musa and Isa. I wish I could live to see the day your people drive you out."

From that night, Muhammad became the Messenger of Allah. The cave of Hira, the mountain that had been silent for so long, became the place where the light of the Qur'an first touched the earth. And the whole world would never be the same again.
The Night Journey and the Ascension

One night, in the deepest hours of the dark, the greatest journey of history began. Allah says: "Exalted is He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque" (Qur'an 17:1). The Prophet traveled from Makkah to Jerusalem in one night.

There, the Prophet met the other prophets — Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and many more — and led them in prayer. Then Allah lifted His beloved servant higher and higher, through the seven skies, to a place where no human had ever gone before.

On that journey, Allah gave the Prophet a gift for the whole ummah: the five daily prayers. Every time a Muslim prays today, they are touching that blessed night. And the Qur'an describes what the Prophet saw: "And he certainly saw him in a second descent" (Qur'an 53:13).

When the Prophet came back and told the people about the journey, the mockers laughed: "One night to Jerusalem and back? Impossible!" But Abu Bakr, the truthful, said at once: "If Muhammad said it, then it is true." That is why Abu Bakr became known as as-Siddiq, the one who confirms the truth.

The night journey teaches every child that Allah's power has no limits. The One who made the stars can carry His servant through the skies. And when the world says "impossible," the believer says: "Allah is able to do all things."
The Two Pledges of Aqabah
The Prophet called his people in Makkah for ten years, and only a few believed. Those believers were hurt every day. Then Allah opened a new door in the city of Yathrib.

Every year in the season of pilgrimage, people from Yathrib came to Makkah. They met the Prophet and heard his beautiful words. Their hearts opened, and they carried the message of Islam back to their city.
In the next year, a small group came by night to a place called Aqabah and made the first pledge. They promised to worship only Allah and to obey the Prophet. Islam began to grow in Yathrib.

A year later, seventy men and two women came by night and made the second pledge. They promised to protect the Prophet as they protected their own children. The Prophet accepted them with a smiling heart.

These were the two pledges of Aqabah. The people of Yathrib became known as the Ansar, the helpers. And Allah promised: "If you help Allah's cause, He will help you and make your feet firm" (Qur'an 47:7).
The Hijrah — A New Home

The enemies of Makkah became more cruel, and they even planned to kill the Prophet. But Allah had a beautiful plan: He commanded the believers to move to the city of Madinah, where kind hearts were waiting to welcome them. The Prophet stayed last, to guide everyone out safely.

When the night came, the enemy surrounded the Prophet's house. But Ali slept in the Prophet's bed, and the Prophet walked out between the enemies while Allah made them unable to see. In the dark of the night, the Prophet set out with his dearest friend, Abu Bakr.

They hid in a cave called Thawr for three days. The enemies came right to the mouth of the cave. Abu Bakr whispered: "If any of them looks down, they will see us." The Prophet said with perfect calm: "Do not grieve — indeed Allah is with us" (Qur'an 9:40).

After the danger passed, the Prophet rode on his camel to Madinah. The people of Madinah had heard of the Prophet and ran out to welcome him, singing songs of joy. Everyone wanted him to stay in their home. So the Prophet said: "Leave the camel free — she will stop where Allah wishes."

Where the camel knelt, the Prophet built the first mosque, and from that day Madinah became the city of light. The Muslims who left Makkah and the Muslims who welcomed them in Madinah became brothers. The hijrah taught the world that leaving your home for Allah is never a loss, it is the greatest gain.
The First Mosque and Brotherhood
When the Prophet came to Madinah, the first thing he did was build a mosque with his own hands. It was a simple place made of clay bricks and palm leaves, but it became the heart of the new city.

The Muslims who came from Makkah were called the Muhajirun, the emigrants. They had left their homes and their money behind. The Muslims of Madinah were called the Ansar, the helpers, and they shared everything with love.

The Prophet joined every Muhajir with an Ansari as a brother. The Ansar said: "Brother, take half of my garden and half of my money." The Muhajirun said: "Just show us the market, and may Allah bless your home."

Allah praised both groups in the Qur'an: "The believers who emigrated and strove in the cause of Allah, and the ones who gave them refuge and helped them — those are the believers in truth" (Qur'an 8:74).
That is how the city of Madinah became one big family. The mosque was not only for prayer; it was also a school where children learned, and a home where the poor were fed. It was the house of mercy.
Badr — The Great Battle and Allah's Help
After the hijrah, the enemies of Islam grew angrier. They gathered a big army and marched toward Madinah to destroy the Muslims. The believers were only a small group, but they trusted Allah.

The Prophet asked his companions to decide, and the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, we will stand with you wherever you go, just as we stand for our own families." So the small Muslim army went out to meet the enemy at the wells of Badr.
The Muslims were only about three hundred, and the enemy was a thousand. But Allah had promised: "Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few" (Qur'an 3:123).

The Prophet prayed all night before the battle. Allah answered: "Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord should support you with three thousand angels?" (Qur'an 3:124). When the morning came, the Muslims fought bravely, and Allah gave them victory.
That day the Muslims learned that numbers do not win battles, Allah does. The victory of Badr was the first great sign that Islam was here to stay.
Uhud — The Archers' Lesson

A year after Badr, the enemy returned with a huge army of three thousand to take revenge. The Muslims went out to meet them near the mountain of Uhud, and the Prophet placed a small group of archers on a hill with a clear order: "Stay here, whatever happens."

At first the Muslims were winning. But when the archers saw that the enemy was running away and the treasure was being gathered, some of them forgot the Prophet's order and left the hill. Then the enemy came from behind, and the battle turned.
Many brave believers fell as martyrs that day, among them the Prophet's dear uncle Hamzah. The Prophet himself was hurt, but he kept saying: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know."
Allah told the believers what had happened: "You indeed lost courage and disagreed about the order and disobeyed" (Qur'an 3:152). The mistake was not an end; it was a lesson.
After the hurt, Allah said: "Do not weaken and do not grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers" (Qur'an 3:139). The believers stood up again, stronger and wiser.
The Trench — Khandaq
After Uhud, the enemies did not give up. They gathered tribes from every side and came with a huge army of ten thousand to finish the Muslims. Madinah was in danger.

The Prophet took advice from his companions. Salman, the wise companion from Persia, suggested: "O Messenger of Allah, in our land, when an enemy comes, we dig a trench around the city." The Prophet loved the idea, and all the believers began to dig with joy.

They dug through cold days and hungry nights. The Prophet worked with his own hands, and the believers sang as they worked. When the enemy arrived, they were surprised: they could not cross the trench with their horses.

Allah says about those days: "When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and eyes became crazed and hearts reached the throats" (Qur'an 33:10). It was a hard time, but the believers did not break.

Then Allah sent a cold wind and fear into the hearts of the enemy. Their army scattered in the night, and the battle of the Trench ended with peace. The believers learned that patience and trust in Allah defeat every siege.
Hudaybiyyah — The Treaty of Peace

In the sixth year after the hijrah, the Prophet's heart longed to visit the Kaaba. He set out with more than a thousand believers, wearing the simple clothes of pilgrimage, carrying no weapons. They only wanted to visit the sacred house of Allah.

But the people of Makkah stopped them at a place called Hudaybiyyah and said: "You may not enter this year." The Muslims were sad, but the Prophet accepted peace talks with patience and sent a message of peace.

While they were waiting, the believers made a pledge under a tree, promising to stay with the Prophet until the end. Allah was pleased with them: "Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree" (Qur'an 48:18).

Then a peace treaty was written: ten years of peace, the Muslims would come for pilgrimage the next year, and anyone who wished could join either side. Many companions were sad, because they wanted to enter Makkah. But the Prophet accepted, and Allah called it a clear victory.

Allah said: "Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory" (Qur'an 48:1). The treaty opened doors of peace, and in the two years that followed, more people entered Islam than in all the years before. Peace was the Prophet's greatest weapon.
Letters to the Kings
After the treaty of peace, the Prophet wanted the whole world to hear about Islam. He sent letters with his trusted companions to the kings of the world, inviting them to worship Allah alone.

He wrote to Heraclius, the king of Rome, to Khosrow, the king of Persia, and to the Negus, the king of Abyssinia. Each letter began with the Prophet's seal and the gentle greeting: "Peace be upon whoever follows the guidance."

In the letters, the Prophet called the people of the Book to the one word that unites everyone: "Say: O People of the Book, come to a word common between us — that we worship none but Allah" (Qur'an 3:64).

Some kings welcomed the message with respect, and some tore the letter. But the news of Islam reached every corner of the earth. The Negus of Abyssinia was so moved that he accepted Islam with all his heart.
The letters taught the world a beautiful lesson: Islam is not only for one city or one people. It is a mercy for all the worlds, and every person is invited to its light.
The Conquest of Makkah
The people of Makkah broke the peace treaty, so the Prophet prepared to enter the city that had hurt him for so long. He marched with ten thousand believers, not to take revenge, but to bring peace.
Allah had announced it: "When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest" (Qur'an 110:1). The city of Makkah opened its doors, and the Prophet entered with his head lowered in humility to Allah.

The Prophet entered the Kaaba and cleaned it from the idols. Then he stood before the people of Makkah, the people who had starved him, mocked him and thrown stones at him, and said the words that melted every heart: "Go — you are free."
The city that had hurt him the most expected punishment, but found mercy. Thousands of people entered Islam that day, and the Kaaba became the pure house of Allah again.
That was the Prophet's greatest victory: not the conquest of a city, but the conquest of hearts. Forgiveness won what swords could never win.
The Farewell Pilgrimage

In the tenth year after the hijrah, the Prophet announced that he would go to Makkah and perform the great pilgrimage of the House of Allah. The happy news spread quickly, and thousands of believers from every town joined him on the road.

Because this was the first and the last Hajj of the Prophet, he taught the people every rite with care: the tawaf around the Kaaba, the sa'i between Safa and Marwah, and the standing on the plain of Arafah. Everyone watched the Prophet and learned each rite from him.

On the day of Arafah, Allah sent down a beautiful verse: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you, and have chosen for you Islam as your religion" (Qur'an 5:3). The religion of the Muslims was now complete.

Then the Prophet stood before the huge gathering and delivered the Farewell Address. He said: protect your lives, your wealth and your honour; be kind to your wives; and remember that all believers are brothers and sisters, and no one is better than another except in piety.

At the end the Prophet asked: "O people, have I delivered the message?" They answered together: "Yes, we bear witness!" Then the Prophet said: "Let the one who is present tell the one who is absent." That was the Farewell Hajj — a precious farewell whose blessed words still guide the believers today.
The Last Days

Not long after the Farewell Hajj, the Prophet fell ill. Even while he was sick, he kept helping the people and speaking to them with gentleness. The believers watched him with love and prayed for his health.

The illness grew heavier, and the Prophet asked Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer. The companions understood that the end was near, and their hearts were filled with sorrow. Abu Bakr led the prayer while the Prophet lay weak and peaceful.

Then the Prophet left this world, in his room, beside his blessed wife Aisha. The news spread and Madinah was filled with tears. Umar could not believe it at first, and he stood in the mosque, telling the people that the Prophet had not passed away.

Then Abu Bakr stood and recited the verse of Allah: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him" (Qur'an 3:144). He said: "Whoever worshipped Muhammad, then Muhammad has passed away; but whoever worshipped Allah — Allah is Ever-Living and never dies." These words calmed every heart.

The believers realized the deep truth: the Prophet had delivered the message, and the religion of Allah was complete. They walked forward on the path he had taught them. The sun of the Prophet set, but the light of his message will never fade.
A Mercy to All the Worlds

Why was the Prophet sent to the world? Allah answers in one beautiful verse: "And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds" (Qur'an 21:107). He was mercy for the orphan, for the poor, for the traveller, for the animals, and for every child who reads his story.

Allah praised his character in the Qur'an: "And indeed, you are of great moral character" (Qur'an 68:4). His whole life was one long lesson in kindness — to the lonely, to the weak, to the sad and to the strangers.

The Prophet is the final messenger of Allah: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets" (Qur'an 33:40). No messenger will come after him, and his message is for every land and every time.

So when you hear the name Muhammad, remember the mercy he brought: a light for the world, a hand for the weak, a smile for the sad, and a path to Allah for everyone. Peace and blessings be upon him and upon all the prophets of Allah.
A Friend Like No Other

Long before Islam, a boy named Abu Bakr lived in Makkah. He was known for a gentle heart, a truthful tongue, and a sharp mind. He grew up near a man named Muhammad ﷺ — a man he trusted completely, even before anyone called him a prophet.

When Muhammad ﷺ began to call people to Islam, Abu Bakr was one of the very first to believe. He did not argue, and he did not delay. His friend Muhammad ﷺ had always been honest, so when the message came, Abu Bakr accepted it with his whole heart.

Because Abu Bakr was well-known and well-loved, many people followed his example. Whole families came into Islam after him. If he spoke well of a man, people would say: “If Abu Bakr trusts him, there is good in him.” So his belief helped many other people believe too.

The Prophet ﷺ loved Abu Bakr very deeply. He said that if he were to take a very close friend, it would be Abu Bakr — but Islam made them even closer than that (Sahih al-Bukhari; Sahih Muslim). That special friendship never changed, right up to the very end.
The One Nobody Could Doubt

One night, the Prophet ﷺ was carried through the heavens — traveling in a single night from Makkah to the far mosque, and then up through the skies. In the morning the people of Makkah laughed at the idea: “That is impossible!”

The people went to Abu Bakr to tell him, expecting him to be surprised too. Instead, Abu Bakr said, “If he said it, then it is true.” That day, the people began to call him as-Siddiq — the one who always confirms the truth.
From then on, the whole community had one name for him: as-Siddiq. And it was a perfect name, because Abu Bakr’s heart never wavered when the Prophet ﷺ spoke. Helping the truth was his greatest joy.
Being as-Siddiq is a lesson for us too: when someone we love and trust tells the truth, our own hearts can learn to believe it with the same quiet confidence.
Freeing the Believers
In early Makkah, the rich enemies would torture new Muslims — especially those who had no protectors. They thought that by hurting them, they could make them give up their belief in Allah.

Abu Bakr could not stand to watch this. He was a wealthy man, so he spent his money buying these servants and setting them free. In the Seerah we read how he freed and cared for a tall, patient believer named Bilal and others too.

The Qur’an speaks of one who gave his wealth to cleanse himself, hoping for no favor in return but only the pleasure of his Lord (Qur’an 92:18–21) — and the early scholars linked this with Abu Bakr and his freeing of the believers.

Freeing a human being and taking care of them is one of the noblest works in Islam. A child today cannot free a servant the way Abu Bakr did, but that child can be kind, generous, and quick to help others — which is the very same caring heart praised by the Prophet ﷺ.
Two in the Cave

When the enemies planned to harm the Prophet ﷺ, Allah told him to leave Makkah for Madeenah. In the dark of the night, Abu Bakr went with him — the two of them slipping out while the whole city slept.

They hid in a mountain-side cave called Thawr. From inside the cave, Abu Bakr could see the enemy running toward it, closer and closer, until they reached the very mouth of the cave. “If they look down, they will see us!” he whispered.

The Prophet ﷺ comforted him and said: “Do not be sad; indeed Allah is with us.” A spider had covered the entrance with its web, and the enemy — never glancing below their feet — passed by without seeing the two hidden travelers.
From that night, the two walked together again, safe under Allah’s protection. With faith like Abu Bakr’s, a person never walks alone; Allah is always with His believing servants.
The First Leader

When the Prophet ﷺ passed away, the Muslims felt very sad, and they came together to decide who would lead them. They looked at one another, because nobody could imagine the community without the Prophet ﷺ.

Then Umar (RA) stepped forward and called the believers to agree on Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr said he was not the best among them, but the people answered: “We do not know anyone better than you.” So Abu Bakr became the first caliph.

Abu Bakr led with a gentle but firm hand. Some people refused to pay the zakah after the Prophet ﷺ had passed away, and Abu Bakr faced them bravely to keep the community of Islam whole. He also asked the companions to gather the words of the Qur’an into one safe book, so that nothing of it would ever be lost.

Abu Bakr ruled only a short while, but he kept Islam safe and complete. When he passed away, the Muslims remembered him as the truest friend of the Prophet ﷺ — the honest leader who carried Islam forward after the Messenger of Allah.
The Sword That Became a Shield

Before he accepted Islam, Umar ibn al-Khattab was one of the strongest and most respected men in Makkah. He was tall, quick-tempered, and utterly fearless, and the people of the city were careful never to cross him. When the Prophet ﷺ began to call people to Allah, Umar was one of the fiercest opponents, and he meant to use all his strength to stop the new faith.

One day Umar became so angry that he took up his sword and walked out across Makkah, determined to confront the Prophet ﷺ himself. On the way a friend stopped him and said: "Before you go anywhere, Umar, look at your own family first." So Umar turned instead toward the house of his sister and her husband — and he learned that they had quietly accepted Islam.

At his sister’s house, Umar heard the words of the Qur’an being read in a gentle voice. He asked to see them, and as he read he came upon a beautiful verse: "Indeed, it is I — I am Allah — there is no god except Me" (Qur’an 20:14). The words entered his heart like cool water on thirsty earth, and he wanted to hear more.

Then and there, Umar went to the Prophet ﷺ and said, plainly and sincerely, that he believed. He accepted Islam with his whole strong heart, and the Muslims of Makkah felt a new safety from that very day. A proud voice that had been raised against the truth now spoke for it.

The sword that Umar had carried against the believers became a shield for them. He used the same courage and boldness to stand beside the companions and to protect the young Muslims who were weak. His story teaches every child that an honest heart can change, and that the strongest hearts belong to the truth of Allah.
The Days of Hardship

When the Muslims came from Makkah to Madinah, they left behind their homes and much of their wealth. The people of Madinah opened their doors and shared whatever they had, and the two groups became one large family. Even so, no one pretended the first months were easy.

There were days when food was scarce and money was lighter than a leaf. Umar never forgot how the Prophet ﷺ would sometimes tie a stone over his own stomach to press down the hunger, living on the simplest meals the earth could give. The believers knew those hard days well — every cup of water was counted and shared.

Yet nobody grumbled or lost heart. The Muhajirun, who had left Makkah, and the Ansar, who welcomed them in Madinah, worked, ate, and prayed as brothers. When one had nothing, the other gave more than what was needed, and the tie of faith grew stronger than jewels.

The hard days taught them patience, and the patience brought fruit. They became grateful for every bite of bread and every cup of water, and their hearts stayed soft even after wealth came. That is the lesson for every child: a thankful heart turns the smallest gift into a great treasure.
A Victory That Looked Like Peace

In the sixth year of the hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ and more than a thousand companions set out for the little journey of umrah, hoping only to visit the Kaaba. They carried no swords and no war plan. But the people of Makkah would not let them enter the city, and the believers stopped at a place called Hudaybiyyah.

For many days the two sides talked, and at last a peace treaty was written down. The Muslims would return home that year and come back next year for their umrah, and for ten years no one would fight the other. To Umar, those old terms looked like giving up, and his chest was filled with sadness and doubt.

Heavy with worry, Umar went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked: "Are we not upon the truth, and are they not upon falsehood?" The Prophet ﷺ answered gently: "I am the Messenger of Allah, and I will not go against His command." Abu Bakr gave the same calm answer, and at last Umar accepted the treaty and found peace.

Then Allah made clear what no one saw, revealing: "Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory" (Qur’an 48:1). A victory with no battle at all. The next year, the Prophet ﷺ and the believers entered Makkah and made their umrah, exactly as the treaty promised.

With peace in time the door of Makkah opened to Islam itself, and many people entered the faith in great numbers. Umar learned — and every child can learn too — that what looks like a bitter wait can be a victory that Allah has hidden inside patience.
Al-Faruq, the One Who Knew the Truth

The believers gave Umar a proud name: al-Faruq, which means the one who sees truth apart from falsehood. Because his mind was sharp and his heart was honest, he went for the right thing and called the wrong thing wrong. That quality of his gave him praise all his life.

Umar was a commander of strict justice but also of soft kindness for the weak. He slept on the floor, ate simple food, and lived in Madinah like one of the working people, even while he protected the rights and property of all with a lion’s courage. If a leader was unfair, even a little, Umar called him back to the path of honesty.

People still remember how the Caliph Umar would wander the lanes of Madinah with a lamp at night, to be sure that no one was hungry and no one had been forgotten. The lonely and the widows and the weary travelers were never a stranger to his lamp. He guarded the city like a shepherd whose head stays alert all night.

Allah invites the believers to this justice: "Hold firmly to justice, being witnesses for Allah, and let the hatred of a nation not cause you to stray from the good" (Qur’an 5:8). A child can follow al-Faruq in a small way: return what you found, read a true word, and be fair to the one who is smaller than you.
The Second and Just Leader

When the first caliph, Abu Bakr, became ill and his time was near, he chose the man he trusted the most to lead the Muslims after him. He chose Umar, and the whole community accepted his choice with love. So when Abu Bakr passed away, Umar became the second Caliph of the Muslims.

Umar ruled a wide land, yet even then he lived like the simplest of the people. His clothes were often patched, and he guarded the public treasury of the Muslims with more care than his own purse. Power did not change him; it only made his heart more careful.

Under his rule the light of Islam went into Syria and Persia and far beyond. He built cities for the Muslim people, laid out roads and marketplaces, and arranged the affairs of the state. He encouraged the believers to count the years from the hijrah, the blessed journey of the Prophet ﷺ, so that time itself would praise that beginning.

Above everything, Umar kept his scales of fairness upright until the very end — nobody, whether rich or weak, was above the law. In every land under his rule, the weak slept in peace, for they knew the Caliph guarded their rights. That is why he remains the symbol of fairness: he was never afraid to tell the truth, and he always sided with the one being wronged.
The Well That Belonged to Everyone

In Madinah, fresh water could be more precious than gold. There was one sweet well called the Well of Rumah, but it belonged to a man who sold its water cup by cup, and the poor people could not drink unless they paid. One day the Prophet ﷺ stood before the companions and said: "Who will buy this well and give it freely to the Muslims?"

Uthman ibn Affan, a wealthy and generous man, agreed at once. He went to the owner and bought the well with his own money — paying every piece the man asked until the well was his. Then he opened it to all the people of Madinah, so that the rich and the poor, the guest and the stranger, could all drink from it freely.

From that day the sweet water of Rumah flowed for every traveller who was thirsty, and the gift of Uthman kept giving long after the seller had counted his coins. The Prophet ﷺ promised that such a gift would be a beloved treasure for Uthman. A gift that helps many people keeps growing in value in front of Allah.

Free water for everyone had become a shared treasure of the whole city. Uthman did not wait to be asked twice — his wealth flowed from his hand into the service of others. That is true generosity: not giving what the heart does not need, but giving quickly and quietly what someone else truly needs.
The Shyness of Uthman

Uthman ibn Affan was a noble, gentle man, and the Prophet ﷺ loved him very much. He was honored to be married to one daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, and when she passed away, the Prophet ﷺ married him to another — so the people praised him as Dhun-Nurayn, "the Possessor of the Two Lights."

Uthman was famous for a beautiful quality: hayaa, the quiet, noble shyness. He spoke softly, lowered his gaze, and never moved forward with a rude or showy word. His modesty about living is a sign of a heart that loves Allah and respects the feelings of others.

The Prophet ﷺ honored him for this, and the companions remember how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say that the light of Uthman was a sign of his goodness and his closeness to the truth. Shyness did not make Uthman weak — it made him gentle, careful, and loved by everyone around him.

Being shy in a good way means guarding the tongue and feeling the feelings of others. A child does not lose courage by being gentle; the two go together, as Uthman showed. Kind eyes, soft words, and a heart that does not wound — that was the good shyness of Uthman ibn Affan.
One Book for the Whole World

The Qur’an is the Book of Allah, and it was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ and then quickly recorded by the scribes of the Prophet and memorized in the hearts of thousands. After the Prophet ﷺ passed away, the Islamic world grew, with Muslims in new lands, and sometimes they recited the same words in their own different ways of reading.

A wise companion named Hudhayfah came to the Caliph Uthman one day with a worried report. The people of the different places had begun to argue over the best way of reading. He urged him: "O leader of the believers, stop the people before they quarrel over the Book of Allah like those before them."

So Uthman gathered the scholars of the Qur’an, among them the great Zaid ibn Thabit, and commanded them to collect the words into one. They gathered all the pages together, checked them against the memory of the memorizers, and wrote out one complete, careful Book in the finest Arabic — the speech of the Prophet ﷺ.

Copies of this one Mushaf were sent to every far city of the Muslims, so that all would read from the same book and no one would lose a single letter of the Revelation. And that Book is the same one that a Muslim opens anywhere on the earth today, whether in Makkah, Madeenah, Cairo, or another home.

Because Uthman cared for the Qur’an and brought it together, the Word of Allah has never been lost. This story teaches: value the Book of Allah, learn it, and hold on to its words. And Uthman is rightly praised as the one who gathered the Qur’an into one.
The Army of the Hard Days

Once the Prophet ﷺ called the believers to a long and difficult expedition in the scorching heat, to the north, toward the land of Tabuk. The road was far, the weather was burning, and the believers had little to spend. It was hard, and only the ones whose hearts were strong stood up ready to go.

The Prophet ﷺ spoke of the great reward for the one who would give generously to equip this struggling army. Uthman came forward and gave with a wide open heart — camels, money, and supplies, until the whole of the expedition was ready thanks to him. He wanted no praise for these, and no return in themselves.

The companions all saw Uthman’s gift, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed a joyful prayer for him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke warmly of the one who gives for the advantage of the Muslims, and the companions remembered that Uthman’s charity would be a treasure for him in the sight of Allah. Whatever good he did after that day, it is a tree that keeps bearing its fruit.

Later, Uthman brought that same spirit to the caliphate. He taught order to the armies of the growing Ummah, divided the new lands with fairness and provided for the soldiers. Strong and organized armies, generous and honest — that was the way of the Prophet ﷺ for the Islamic rule that went out beyond.

Generosity is measured not in coins but in the readiness of the heart. Uthman equipped the army so completely that the entire team could move forward, and the hearts of the believers were filled with trust. A child can give a coin, share a snack, or welcome a new friend — that is the same generous spirit at work on their little scale.
The Third Leader of the Muslims

When the second caliph, Umar, passed away, the great companions gathered together to choose the next leader of the believers. After open and honest counsel they agreed with one heart on Uthman. So Uthman became the third Caliph, gently and humbly, the open book of his hands extended to all.

Uthman carried the justice and the order laid down by Abu Bakr and Umar, and he added his own gentle and generous spirit. He enlarged the Prophet’s mosque in Madinah and planned the streets and houses of the city, while at home he lived simply and kept nothing but a quiet heart.

During his time the light of the Islamic state reached new horizons and lands. The call of the faith crossed rivers and mountains, and the pattern of his gentle, careful leadership strengthened the kingdom that wanted peace and faith on both of them.

Above all, Uthman is the champion of the Qur’an: he made the Book one, and by that he held the whole Ummah together. A child today can open his own Mushaf and find the care of Uthman in it — together with a sweet well for the thirsty and an open hand for the believers. That is Uthman: the shy, the generous, the hero of the two lights and of the one Book.
A Boy in the Prophet’s House

Long ago, Makkah had a year when the rain did not come and the ground grew hard and dry. Life was very hard for everyone, including a good uncle of the Prophet ﷺ named Abu Talib, who had many young ones to feed.
The Prophet ﷺ always helped people, so he took his little cousin Ali into his own home. Ali grew up eating, sleeping, and learning beside the most honest man in all of Makkah.
From a very small age, Ali watched everything the Prophet ﷺ did. He saw how gently he spoke to the little ones, how kindly he treated his neighbors, and how he never, ever told a lie.
Because of this, the Prophet ﷺ shaped the man Ali would become. Years later, everyone who knew him said the same thing: growing up in the Prophet’s house had filled his heart with light.
The First of the Children

When the Prophet ﷺ began to call people to worship Allah alone, some of his dearest listeners were his own family. Among them was a boy — Ali — who was still young, standing at the edge between childhood and the story of Islam.

One day the Prophet ﷺ asked his family to be the first to accept the message. Ali did not wait, and he did not ask for more signs. He already loved the Prophet ﷺ so much that his heart said “I believe” right away.
The Seerah tells us that among the boys and girls of Makkah, Ali was the first child to accept Islam. He was only around ten years old, but his courage stood taller than many grown-ups.
Being first is not about being the biggest or the strongest. Ali showed that even a child can lead the way with a brave heart, and that loving Allah from a young heart is a very real thing.

In those very first days, the household of the Prophet ﷺ was just three people: the Prophet ﷺ, his wife Khadijah, and young Ali. Together they carried the first small light of Islam before anyone else joined.
The Brave Fighter

When the believers moved to Madinah, enemies from Makkah still came to fight them. In the great battlefield of Badr, Ali was still a young man, yet he stood in the lines of the fighters with a heart as steady as the strongest shield.
At Badr, a small and faithful army of Muslims faced many enemies, and Allah gave them a wonderful victory. Ali fought with all his strength, protecting his Prophet ﷺ and the believers beside him.

Years later, when it came to the strong forts of Khaybar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “I will give the flag tomorrow to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.” Everyone could hardly wait for the morning.

The next day, the Prophet ﷺ called for no one but Ali and placed the flag in his hand. With the flag in hand, Ali said he would first call the enemy to Islam — and only if they refused would there be a fight for the truth.
That day Ali carried the flag as boldly as a lion, and the people began to call him the lion of Allah. All his strength, he always said, belonged not to himself but to Allah.
Deep Praise From the Prophet ﷺ

The Prophet ﷺ loved Ali very much and praised him on many special days. During a very long journey, Ali had to stay behind in Madinah for a while, and some troublemakers whispered: “Look, he was left behind!”

Ali hurried after the Prophet ﷺ to explain. The Prophet ﷺ then said to him those famous words: “Are you not satisfied to be to me like Harun to Musa?” — like Aaron, the brother and helper of the prophet Moses, peace be upon them.
And the Prophet ﷺ added the deepest of them all: “But there is no prophet after me.” For a while, Ali’s place beside the Messenger of Allah was the closest a companion could ever reach.

Makkah called the Prophet ﷺ “the trustworthy one” even before Islam, and he trusted Ali the same way. When they were together, the town knew that whatever the Prophet ﷺ said, and whatever Ali agreed to, could always be believed.

Such praise from the one he loved carried Ali for his whole life. It reminds us that when someone we love speaks into our hearts with kindness and trust, it can lift us higher than we ever knew we could go.
Wise and Fair for Allah

Many people remember Ali only as a swordsman. But the Prophet ﷺ also trusted him as a judge and a teacher, and he sent him to a distant land to lead the people. Ali had hands that could fight, and a heart that loved fairness.

When the Prophet ﷺ sent Ali to judge between people, he gave him this advice: listen to both sides before deciding, so that no innocent person is ever harmed. Ali carried those words like a lamp in his heart.

Everyone could see how fairly Ali decided. He never favored the rich over the poor, and he never took the side of his own family over a stranger. His wisdom flowed from his love of Allah, which made people trust him.
Ali also taught his students that a sharp mind is a person’s best weapon. Strength can win a single fight, but knowledge and fairness keep peace between people for a whole lifetime.

So Ali’s real title is not only “the Brave.” He is also “the Wise.” Fighting was just a small part of his story — the true story is a boy who grew into a man whose fairness and gentle mind made a whole generation trust him.
A Fair and Honest Merchant

Long before Islam, a girl named Khadijah grew up in Makkah. As she became an adult, she proved to be one of the wisest merchants in the whole city, sending her caravans to faraway lands loaded with fine goods.

She was so honest and pure in her dealings that people called her at-Tahira, “the pure one.” Even though she was very wealthy, she never cheated a single customer and she always treated her helpers with kindness.
When she needed a trustworthy man to lead one of her great trading journeys, everyone told her the same name: Muhammad ﷺ, the man the whole city called al-Ameen, “the trustworthy one.”

Muhammad ﷺ led the journey with perfect honesty, and it returned with good profit. But the true treasure was something else: Khadijah saw his beautiful character with her own eyes, and her respect and love for him grew very deep.
The First to Believe

One day the Prophet ﷺ returned home carrying news that would change the world: Allah had made him the Messenger for all of mankind. His dearest wife Khadijah sat beside him, and his heart needed someone to hold the secret.

Khadijah listened, and she did not hesitate for a single moment. She was the very first person in the entire world to accept Islam — before Abu Bakr, before Ali, before anyone. She said: “I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah.”

She did not need fireworks or miracles to believe. She had lived with this man for many years, and she knew with certainty that he had never told a lie in his whole life. So when he spoke the truth, her whole heart trusted him.

Her quick belief was a great blessing to the Prophet ﷺ. When the city of Makkah was difficult and most people refused him, the one part of the world where he always felt believed and loved was the home of Khadijah.

The very first “yes” in the story of Islam did not come from a grand hall or a mighty king. It came quietly from the gentle heart of a wife, inside a small home — and that first yes carried the whole religion on its back.
Warmth in a Dark Hour

At the very beginning of revelation, the Prophet ﷺ came down from the mountain cave trembling, carrying a beautiful but enormous weight. He hurried into his home saying: “Cover me! Cover me!” and Khadijah wrapped him in a blanket.

Then Khadijah spoke the most comforting words found anywhere in the stories of Makkah: “By Allah, He will never put you to shame. You keep your family ties, you carry the burden of others, you help the poor, and you give to the needy.”

She confirmed his heart and then took him to her wise and elderly relative, a man who knew the old scriptures. He said to both of them: the same angel that came to Moses has now come to him, and he is the prophet of this people.
From that night on, the Prophet ﷺ knew that he was not alone on this new road. The revelation fell onto his heart like heavy rain — but Khadijah was the kind roof that kept him warm and safe.

Every child who loves the story of the first revelation should also learn this beautiful part: when the mountain shook and the darkness closed, the Prophet ﷺ found his light in the comfort of Khadijah’s kind words.
The Year of Sorrow

For many years the Prophet ﷺ and his family carried their faith under hard trials in the city of Makkah. The enemies treated his people harshly, and the one big protector, his kind uncle Abu Talib, passed away after many years of watching over him.

Then, very soon after, Khadijah’s gentle body became weak, and she returned to Allah. In one short stretch of time, the Prophet ﷺ had lost the two people who had protected and comforted him his whole life — and the people called it the “Year of Sorrow.”

The believers recalled that the Prophet ﷺ missed Khadijah with such a deep and long love that even years later, when her old friends came to visit, tears of memory would gather right at the edge of his eyes.

That hardest of years taught the believers about patience. From the Prophet ﷺ they learned that even a heart filled with grief never stops trusting Allah and never stops serving the mission, and that the year of the hardest seasons still only passes in a moment.

We honor Khadijah every time we retell the early beauty of Islam. Her years helped the Prophet ﷺ stand, and her passing taught the whole world that great love does not end — it only changes where it rests.
He Never Stopped Loving Her

Long after Khadijah passed away, the Prophet ﷺ married again, and one of his wives, Aisha, shared a famous honest secret: even though she had never met her, she felt the loving shadow of Khadijah in their home.

Whenever the Prophet ﷺ cooked a sheep or received a gift, he sent part of it to her families and old friends — quietly, no fanfare — so that the memory of his first wife would never grow thirsty in the world.

One day he mentioned her to Aisha, and Aisha, in her loving teasing, said she wished she could be like her. The Prophet ﷺ did not scold her; he just nodded, and reminded them both that the treasure he treasured most in marriage was the love of a true and gentle heart.

Because of this, the whole world remembers him as a faithful husband. He remembered Khadijah’s kindness after she was gone, and did not let it grow cold — he kept sharing that kindness with her friends and family.

Kindness that we remember and share, as the Prophet ﷺ shared Khadijah’s, is the kind of love that never grows tired. We can honor this precious mother of the believers by being soft, honest, and generous — just as she was.
A Heart That Would Not Break

Bilal was a tall, strong man who was a servant in Makkah. When he accepted Islam, his owner grew very angry. The owner threw Bilal on the hot sand and placed a heavy stone on his chest, hoping Bilal would give up his faith.

But Bilal only repeated one word again and again: “Ahad, Ahad — One, One (Allah).” The hotter the day, the stronger his words became. The stones and the heat could hurt his body, but they could never touch his heart.
The Seerah tells us how much goodness Bilal had inside him. Even while he was hurting, he did not become angry at people. He only remembered Allah, because His love was stronger than any pain.

Bilal’s story teaches children a very strong lesson: your heart can be worth more than your physical strength. When we hold on to Allah even through small troubles, our hearts grow as strong as the hearts of the heroes of Islam.
Bought and Freed by Abu Bakr

Abu Bakr (RA) could not watch his believing brother suffer. He gave money to Bilal’s owner and freed him, so that Bilal could finally stand up, tall and free, and praise his Lord out loud without fear.
Bilal the student was a free man, and free same heart he had kept in confinement came out whole. He found his place beside the Prophet ﷺ, close to him night and day, loving him more and more.

Some people once said that Abu Bakr had bought Bilal for a small profit, so the Prophet ﷺ corrected them: “If you underpaid him, we would repay it; if you overpaid him, we would accept him.” And he made sure everyone knew that Abu Bakr’s payment-turing was accepted (Sahih al-Bukhari; Seerah).

So freedom came twice for Bilal: first his body was freed, and then his voice was freed to praise. And freedom is a blessing we should always be thankful for, and use to worship Allah and help others.
The First Voice of the Adhan

When the Muslims moved to Madeenah, the Prophet ﷺ wanted a special sign to call people to the prayer. One night, a friend of the Prophet saw the adhan in a dream — the beautiful words that call “Allah is Greatest, Allah is Greatest… Come to prayer!”

The Prophet ﷺ loved the idea, and told Bilal to rise and call the adhan with these words. So the first voice of the adhan ever heard in Islam belonged to Bilal, with his deep and sweet voice calling the city to the prayer.

The Prophet ﷺ said that the mu’adhins — the people who call the prayer — are the longest ones in the necks on the Day of Judgment, honored because their voices spent their whole lives calling people to Allah (Sahih Muslim).

Every time a child hears the adhan today, they are hearing the echo of Bilal’s voice through the world. The same turn to the prayer is the one he called with his honest heart in the very first years of Islam.
The Voice Behind the Prophet

Bilal stayed close to the Prophet ﷺ every year of his life. When the Prophet called prayer, Bilal called, and when the Messenger traveled, Bilal went with him, and his famous shoe threw the sand of Madeenah, the Prophet ﷺ heard him in Paradise and smiled.

The Prophet ﷺ once told Bilal that he had heard the sound of his steps ahead of him in Paradise because of a beautiful prayer Bilal had learned. Being a companion so near the Prophet ﷺ was the biggest reward a human heart could hold.

When the Prophet ﷺ passed away, Bilal’s voice became heavy. He asked the first caliph, Abu Bakr (RA), to let him stop calling the adhan in Madinah, because every call to prayer reminded him of the Messenger ﷺ he loved best of all.

Today the name Bilal reminds Muslims of a believer who lost everything except Allah — and from that poverty Allah raised him to honor. He is a shining proof that Allah chooses His servants not by their worldly wealth, but by the purity of their hearts.
Legacy and Lesson
After the Prophet ﷺ died, the companions carried what they had learned outward — to new towns, to their children, and to whoever asked how to pray, give, or forgive.
Bilal ibn Rabah's legacy is not only a story to remember. It is a way of acting that is still available: truthful speech, patient hardship, generous hands.

A Warrior Before Islam

Khalid was a brave and clever man from Makkah. Even before Islam he was famous for his courage and his skill in battle. At the battle of Uhud, he commanded the cavalry that passed beside the Muslims, and for a while his boldness shook the believers.

But in the middle of the battlefield, Khalid also noticed something strange and beautiful. Even when the Muslims began to stumble, they did not run or break. They gathered around their Prophet ﷺ and around the truth, and that silent strength stayed in Khalid’s mind for a long time.

Years later, when the two armies met again at the trench, the same feeling came back to him. The truth did not win with endless weapons; it won because it was truly the truth, and Khalid’s own heart began to lean toward it more and more.

We can learn from Khalid that a person’s past is not his future. Where a soul was headed yesterday does not decide today. The heart can be turned around, and Khalid’s chapter shows us exactly that in a way almost no other story does.
The Day He Came to the Prophet
In the year of the treaty, the peace of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, Khalid felt his heart ready. He rode to the Prophet ﷺ together with his brother, and both of them were welcomed warmly into Islam.

The Prophet ﷺ received him with a smile and a free heart. The same hands that had held a sword against the believers became hands raised in prayer, and the same courage turned to the side of the faith.

From that day, Khalid used his talent — the same talent he had used on a bad side — now completely for the good. When Allah turns a heart, He does not discard its gifts; He aims the same gifts at the right targets.
It was the most important victory in Khalid’s whole life, and it was not won on any battlefield. It was won quietly, inside his chest, the day he said yes to the truth.
The Sword of Allah

Khalid soon became one of the bravest soldiers of the Prophet ﷺ. At the battle of Mutah, when the first great commanders of the Muslims fell one after another, Khalid stepped up and took the banner, keeping the Muslim army true night of those days.

The Prophet ﷺ was overjoyed and thanks a praiseworthy name for him: Khalid is the Sword of Allah against the enemies. The whole world of Islam would remember his name forever as "Sayf Allah," the Sword of Allah.

A sword is not always a symbol of breaking. Khalid used his courage to protect the people, guard the faith, and face those who wanted to harm the believers. That is the story of a hero — strength turned into mercy and safety.

Every child has some own skill — a strong arm, a loud patient, a quick mind. What Khalid’s life says is: place your skill into Allah’s hands, and it will be shaped into something that protects and heals and helps the whole world.
Serving Faith with a Second Courage

After the Prophet ﷺ passed away, Khalid kept serving the community under the first caliph, Abu Bakr (RA). He led the Muslim armies through the dark days when several tribes tried to end their faith once more — pushing the confusion away with his courage.

He commanded the armies of the believers in the wars of apostasy, and then the victories in Syria and beyond. Little by little, through his plan and bravery, great lands came together under justice and the fear/prayer of Allah.

For all his strength, Khalid was a man who the heart. In his last days he asked Allah for a death of a hero, and his old friends remember how he cared his treasures away, avoiding the wealth and the vanity like a saadiq.
Khalid finished as he had lived — strong, humble, and true. The sword of Allah was finally resting in the hand of the One who manages every soldier and every heart.
Legacy and Lesson
After the Prophet ﷺ died, the companions carried what they had learned outward — to new towns, to their children, and to whoever asked how to pray, give, or forgive.
Khalid ibn al-Walid's legacy is not only a story to remember. It is a way of acting that is still available: truthful speech, patient hardship, generous hands.
